issues.claim: after a family who held land here
issues.problem: Marish commemorates one woman, not a family.
issues.correct: 'Marish or Maries commemorates Christiana de Marecis who held the manor for a short time in the reign of Edward I' (13th century).
issues.suggested_text: It comes from Old English lang, long, and lēah, a clearing in a wood. The old village is sometimes called Langley Marish, after Christiana de Marecis, who held the manor in the 13th century.

issues.claim: a London merchant who died in 1627
issues.correct: He was an attorney and clerk in the Court of Wards and Liveries; died January 1627.
issues.suggested_head: Named after Edward Latymer, a London lawyer who died in 1627.

issues.claim: The city of Leicester takes its name from a Celtic tribe and 'ceaster', a Roman town.
issues.problem: Sources do not call the Ligore a Celtic tribe; they were a people named after the River Ligor (Soar), whose name is of uncertain, probably Brittonic, origin.
issues.correct: First element is the Ligore, a people named after the River Ligor (now the Soar); second is Old English ceaster.
issues.suggested_text: The square was laid out in front of his house in the 1670s. The city of Leicester is named after the Ligore, the people of the River Soar, and 'ceaster', a Roman town.

issues.claim: The railway company built the line through here in the 1890s, and the road beside the station took its name.
issues.problem: Could not confirm that Midland Road was named after the railway. Also, the line was built by the Tottenham and Forest Gate Railway, a joint company of the Midland and the London, Tilbury & Southend, not the Midland alone. Checked the Wikipedia station page and a web search.
issues.correct: Station opened 9 July 1894 on the Tottenham and Forest Gate Railway as 'Leyton'; renamed Leyton Midland Road on 1 May 1949. Wikipedia gives no origin for the road name.
issues.suggested_text: The line, part-owned by the Midland Railway, opened here in 1894. The road beside the station is named after the railway company.

issues.claim: Brunel's railway bridge here, opened in 1838
issues.problem: The bridge was finished in 1838 but opened in 1839.
issues.suggested_text: It comes from Old English mægden, maiden, and hȳth, a landing place on the Thames. Brunel's railway bridge here, finished in 1838, has the flattest brick arches ever built.

issues.claim: has two of the widest and flattest brick arches ever built
issues.problem: The source says the arches were the widest and flattest in the world when built. Only 'flattest' is said to hold today.
issues.correct: 'The widest and flattest in the world' at construction; 'the arches of the structure remain the flattest ever constructed'.
issues.suggested_text: It comes from Old English mægden, maiden, and hȳth, a landing place on the Thames. Brunel's railway bridge here, finished in 1838, has the flattest brick arches ever built.

issues.claim: Named after the manor house of the manor of Little Ilford.
issues.problem: Wrong manor. The name comes from a house built for the lord of the manor of West Ham, not Little Ilford's manor house.
issues.correct: Hidden London: the suburb 'took its name from the manor house built around 1810' for the lord of the manor of West Ham, on his Hamfrith estate (it survives in Gladding Road). The area had been part of the manor of Little Ilford. Wikipedia gives no origin.
issues.suggested_head: Named after a manor house built around 1810 on the Hamfrith estate.

issues.claim: It stands on the site of an earlier house called The More, which belonged to Cardinal Wolsey.
issues.problem: The mansion is not on the site of The More. It was built on a hill south-west of the old palace, inside its deer park.
issues.correct: 'It is called Moor Park Mansion because it is in the old park of the Manor of the More'; built 'on the hill to the southwest of the old palace, within the deer park'. (Wolsey did own The More.)
issues.suggested_text: It stands in the old park of The More, a palace that once belonged to Cardinal Wolsey. The station opened in 1910 as Sandy Lodge.

issues.claim: a coaching inn, the New Cross
issues.problem: The inn was called the Golden Cross, not the New Cross. The 'older wayside cross' idea is not in the sources.
issues.correct: 'New Cross is believed to have taken its name from a coaching house originally known as the Golden Cross'. A turnpike gate named after the inn spread the name.
issues.suggested_head: Probably named after a coaching inn, the Golden Cross, on the road to Kent and Dover.
issues.suggested_text: A toll gate near the inn later spread the name to the whole area. Goldsmiths, part of the University of London, is next to the station.

issues.claim: The station opened in 1947, when the Central line took over a branch railway.
issues.problem: The station is older. 1947 is when Central line trains started.
issues.correct: Opened by the Great Eastern Railway on 1 May 1903; Central line services from 14 December 1947.
issues.suggested_text: The name is medieval. The station opened in 1903, and the Central line took it over in 1947.

issues.claim: about two miles north-east of Greenwich itself
issues.problem: Too far. In a straight line the station is about 1.3 miles (2 km) north-east of Greenwich town centre (worked out from map coordinates). No source gives two miles.
issues.correct: About 1.3 miles in a straight line, at the northern tip of the borough on the Greenwich Peninsula.
issues.suggested_text: It was first recorded in the early 10th century. The station, opened in 1999, is just over a mile north-east of Greenwich itself, next to what was built as the Millennium Dome.

issues.problem: Wrong Old English word. Næs means a headland. The source gives nēos, nose.
issues.correct: 'derived from the Old English nēos = nose and dūn = hill'.
issues.suggested_text: It comes from Old English nēos, nose, and dūn, hill. The station opened in 1880 as Kingsbury & Neasden.

issues.claim: The station opened in 1908 as Northfield Halt.
issues.problem: Sources disagree. Wikipedia says it 'opened as Northfield (Ealing) on 16 April 1908'. The Little Ealing History site calls it 'Northfield Halt'.
issues.correct: Opened 16 April 1908 as Northfield (Ealing) (Wikipedia) or Northfield Halt (local history society). Renamed Northfields & Little Ealing in 1911 and Northfields in 1932.
issues.suggested_text: The fields were farmland until houses were built in the early 20th century. The station opened in 1908 as Northfield.

issues.claim: which takes its name from the oaks of Enfield Chase
issues.problem: The source says Oakwood Park is named after a house, not oak trees.
issues.correct: Oakwood Park was 'named after Oak Lodge', a building in its grounds. Station: opened 13 March 1933 as Enfield West, renamed Enfield West (Oakwood) 1934, Oakwood 1 September 1946.
issues.suggested_head: Named after Oakwood Park, which took its name from a house called Oak Lodge.
issues.suggested_text: Nearby Enfield Chase was a royal hunting ground. The station opened in 1933 as Enfield West and became Oakwood in 1946.
